content: Vasa praevia is an obstetric complication in which fetal blood vessels cross or are located very close to the internal cervical os. These vessels are contained within the membranes and are not supported by the umbilical cord or placental tissue. As a result, they are at significant risk of rupture when the membranes rupture. In vasa praevia, the fetal vessels traverse the membranes over the internal cervical os. These vessels may originate from a velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord or may connect an accessory (succenturiate) placental lobe to the main placental disk. If these vessels rupture, the bleeding occurs from the fetoplacental circulation. This can lead to rapid and severe fetal blood loss (exsanguination), which often results in fetal death. Vasa praevia is more commonly associated with certain conditions, including velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord, the presence of accessory placental lobes, and multiple gestations. The diagnosis of vasa praevia is rarely confirmed before delivery. However, it may be suspected during pregnancy if an antenatal ultrasound with color-flow Doppler imaging shows a blood vessel crossing the membranes over the internal cervical os. In most cases, the diagnosis is confirmed after delivery through an examination of the placenta and fetal membranes. Unfortunately, in many instances, the fetus has already died by the time the diagnosis is made. This is because the blood loss from ruptured fetal vessels (e.g., approximately 300 mL) represents a significant proportion of the fetal blood volume, which is approximately 80-100 mL per kilogram of fetal weight (e.g., around 300 mL for a 3-kilogram fetus). The treatment for vasa praevia typically involves immediate emergency cesarean delivery to prevent fetal death. The use of oxytocin is absolutely contraindicated in cases of vasa praevia.
